title: Regular sections and transverse direct sums
statement:
In the finite setting [def-pur-conventions], let $T$ be a separated finite-type $k$-scheme and $F$ a locally free $\mathcal O_T$-module of constant rank $r\geq0$ [def-amb-finite-locally-free-module]. Put $F^\vee=\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal O_T}(F,\mathcal O_T)$, using the ordinary sheaf Hom [def-pur-sheaf-hom] on the Zariski site. Thus over an open $U$ its sections are $\mathcal O_U$-linear maps $F|_U\to\mathcal O_U$. A frame $F|_U\cong\mathcal O_U^{\oplus r}$ gives the dual frame by the coordinate projections, so $F^\vee|_U\cong\mathcal O_U^{\oplus r}$. Write $E(F)=\underline{\operatorname{Spec}}_T\operatorname{Sym}(F^\vee)$ with projection $p$ and zero section $z$, by [def-pur-vector-bundle-zero-section] applied to the locally free module $F^\vee$ (not $F$).

A section $s$ means an element of $\Gamma(T,F)=F(T)$. Define $\operatorname{ev}_s:F^\vee\to\mathcal O_T$ on $U$ by $\lambda\mapsto\lambda(s|_U)$. The unique algebra map $\operatorname{Sym}(F^\vee)\to\mathcal O_T$ extending $\operatorname{ev}_s$ is given by [lem-weil-pbc-quasi-coherent-symmetric-algebra-core]; under [lem-weil-pbc-affine-morphism-relative-spec](3) it defines a $T$-morphism, also written $s:T\to E(F)$. Conversely such a morphism gives a linear map $F^\vee\to\mathcal O_T$; in a frame this map has the values $a_1,\ldots,a_r$ on the dual basis and hence gives the section $\sum_i a_i e_i$. On overlaps this expression is characterized by $\lambda(s)=\operatorname{ev}_s(\lambda)$ for all dual sections, so it agrees and glues. This identifies sections of $F$ with sections of $p$.

Define the zero scheme by the fibre product [def-pc-fibre-product]
$$
Z(s)=T\times_{E(F),s,z}T,
$$
with its morphism to $T$. Its ideal sheaf is the image of $\operatorname{ev}_s$. More explicitly, on an affine frame open $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum], with $s|_U=\sum_i a_i e_i$, the symmetric algebra has coordinates $A[x_1,\ldots,x_r]$ by [lem-weil-pbc-quasi-coherent-symmetric-algebra-affine] and [lem-weil-pbc-symmetric-algebra-free-module-polynomial]. The section and zero section send $x_i$ to $a_i$ and $0$, respectively. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra] their fibre product has ring
$$
A\otimes_{A[x_1,\ldots,x_r]}A\cong A/(a_1,\ldots,a_r).
$$
Indeed the tensor relations equate $a_i\otimes1$ with $1\otimes0$, and the mutually inverse maps send $a\otimes b$ to $ab$ modulo $(a_1,\ldots,a_r)$ and $\bar a$ to $a\otimes1$. Its ideal is $(a_1,\ldots,a_r)$, also the image of evaluation on the dual basis. These quotient charts show that $Z(s)\to T$ is a closed immersion by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-affine-cover-criterion](2).

The section is regular if for every $x\in Z(s)$ there is a local frame of $F$ at $x$ in which its $r$ component germs form an $\mathcal O_{T,x}$-regular sequence [def-weil-pbc-regular-sequence]: multiplication by each germ on the quotient by its predecessors is injective, and the final quotient is nonzero. No smoothness of $T$ or of $Z(s)$ over $k$ is part of this condition. The condition at an empty zero locus is vacuous. In rank zero $E(F)=T$, the unique section is zero, and $Z(s)=T$; its empty component sequence is regular at every point since a local ring at a scheme point is nonzero.

Let $G$ also be locally free of constant rank $e\geq0$, and let $s$ of $F$ and $t$ of $G$ be regular sections. A transverse direct sum means that at every $x\in Z(s)\cap Z(t)$ there are local frames of $F$ and $G$ in which the concatenated component germs of $(s,t)$ form an $\mathcal O_{T,x}$-regular sequence. The direct sum is the sheaf with sections $F(U)\oplus G(U)$ on each open $U$. Its zero scheme is the scheme-theoretic intersection, meaning the fibre product $Z(s)\times_TZ(t)$. In simultaneous affine frames the components are $a_1,\ldots,a_r,b_1,\ldots,b_e$ and both schemes have ring $A/(a_1,\ldots,a_r,b_1,\ldots,b_e)$: by [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra] the intersection ring is $A/(a_i)\otimes_A A/(b_j)$, with the same multiplication and $\bar a\mapsto\bar a\otimes1$ inverse maps. These identifications are induced by the fibre-product projections and therefore agree on overlaps.
